paras: The shooting of George Carter took place in King George County, Virginia, in August 1890, when Randolph Inscoe, a white man, shot Carter, a Black man, after a quarrel and left him with what the papers called a mortal wound. Inscoe was arrested, examined before a magistrate and released on bail to await the next term of the County Court. Richmond dispatches attributed the quarrel to "political talk and impudence on the part of the negro" in a hotly contested congressional district, while a later report from the county seat traced it to a dispute over hauling wood.

The first reports placed the trouble in the Eighth Congressional District, where, according to a Fredericksburg correspondent, "great excitement prevails as to the candidates" for Congress. According to the King George Court House correspondent of the Richmond Times, both men were hauling wood to the river near St. Paul's church, and Carter complained that Inscoe was putting wood in the road and cutting him off from the shore.

The first account, a special telegram from Fredericksburg dated August 13 and printed in both the Richmond Dispatch and the Richmond Times, said the two men had quarreled the day before and that Inscoe, "closely pressed" by Carter, drew a pistol and shot him. Both papers added that he had acted, "it is said," in self-defense.

The King George special, dated a day later, gave a fuller and different sequence. In the quarrel, it said, Carter threw Inscoe down and bit him twice on the face; Inscoe then went home for his gun and, about two hours later, met Carter and shot him in the thigh and abdomen. That report called the wounds "probably fatal."

Inscoe was arrested and brought before a magistrate. At the preliminary examination there was, the Times correspondent wrote, "much conflicting testimony concerning the shooting," though all the witnesses agreed that Carter had been "extremely abusive" to Inscoe and had threatened his life. Justice Benjamin Weaver released Inscoe on $100 bail, conditioned on his appearance at the next term of the County Court.

The Fredericksburg dispatch reported "much excitement" among both Black and white residents of the neighborhood and said that "serious trouble is apprehended." No later report of Carter's death, an inquest, an indictment or a trial was found in the coverage through September 1890.

The coverage found came only from three Virginia papers, the Richmond Dispatch, the Richmond Times and the Alexandria Gazette, on August 14 and 15. The Dispatch ran the Fredericksburg telegram under the headlines "A Negro Mortally Wounded" and "Political Insolence the Cause," described Inscoe as "a highly-respectable white man," and identified Carter as "a negro." The Times printed the same dispatch at the end of a Fredericksburg column devoted to a society wedding, and its news summary reduced the episode to the line "Randolph Inseoc shot a negro in King George county," without naming Carter. The Alexandria Gazette condensed the item into its "Virginia News" column, dating the shooting to "Tuesday" and dropping the self-defense claim and the description of Inscoe's standing, but keeping the explanation of "political talk and impudence."

The Times's follow-up from King George Court House, headed "Shooting Affray in the County-Cause of the Difficulty," labeled the men "(white)" and "(colored)" and set aside the political explanation in favor of the wood dispute. Every account found appeared in the white press, none gave Carter's own version of the quarrel, and no coverage in the Black press was found.

The reports differ on the cause, the sequence and the date of the shooting. The Fredericksburg dispatch gave the political talk and Carter's "impudence" as a rumor, whereas the King George correspondent, writing from the county seat after the magistrate's hearing, described a quarrel over wood and the road to the shore. The first account had Inscoe shoot while "closely pressed," in self-defense; the later one had him fetch a gun and shoot Carter two hours after the fight. The Fredericksburg dispatch of August 13 and the Gazette placed the shooting on Tuesday, August 12, while the King George special dated August 14 said it happened "About 12 o'clock yesterday," that is, on August 13.

bases: One white man, Randolph Inscoe, shot George Carter after a personal quarrel; no mob, band or crowd took part (A2, A5).

The Fredericksburg special (A2, A4, condensed in A1) and an independent King George Court House special (A5, A6) agree that Inscoe shot and gravely wounded Carter and was bailed, though they differ on cause, sequence and date.

framing.detail: The Dispatch headed the item 'A Negro Mortally Wounded ... Political Insolence the Cause', called Inscoe 'a highly-respectable white man' and reported self-defense.

The Times's King George follow-up, 'Shooting Affray in the County', described a dispute over wood and reported that Inscoe fetched a gun and shot Carter two hours later, alongside witnesses' claims against Carter.
The Alexandria Gazette condensed the special into its 'Virginia News' column, keeping 'impudence on the part of the negro' but dropping the self-defense and 'highly-respectable' language.
